query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled, low‐temperature annealing treatment that induces the precipitation of coherent nano-scale L12 intermetallic particles within the FCC phase of a eutectic HEA will simultaneously increase strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy in the as-cast condition exhibiting a lamellar dual-phase (e.g., FCC + B2) microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply a low-temperature annealing treatment optimized to precipitate fine, coherent L12 particles within the ductile FCC lamellae.
generation.conditions: The treatment is conducted under conditions that avoid significant coarsening (e.g., controlled annealing temperatures and times), with mechanical testing under quasi-static tensile loading at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent nano-scale L12 precipitates distributed within the FCC phase, leading to refined microstructure and effective phase boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The fine L12 precipitates provide obstacles to dislocation motion (via mechanisms such as Orowan dislocation bowing), which increases yield strength. Simultaneously, the uniform dispersion of these nanoscale precipitates refines the microstructure and promotes a more homogeneous distribution of plastic strain, thereby enhancing ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast baseline, the annealed alloy is expected to exhibit an increased yield strength (potentially on the order of tens of percent improvement, though the exact value is uncertain) while either maintaining or improving uniform ductility.
generation.baseline: As-cast eutectic HEA specimen with its initial lamellar dual-phase microstructure.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected in eutectic HEAs that exhibit a lamellar structure amenable to L12 precipitation; if the annealing treatment parameters are not optimized, coarsening of precipitates may occur, negating the intended ductility enhancement.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of strength and ductility improvements and the narrow processing window for optimal L12 precipitation remain to be established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of eutectic HEA samples in the as-cast state and subject them to a range of low-temperature annealing treatments with controlled variations in time and temperature. Characterize the microstructure using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to verify the formation and distribution of coherent L12 precipitates, then perform quasi-static tensile tests at room temperature.
measurements: Precipitate size distribution and volume fraction
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If none of the annealed samples simultaneously exhibit a statistically significant increase in yield strength and ductility over the as-cast baseline (or if precipitate coarsening reduces ductility), then the hypothesis will be refuted.

cited_evidence.text: Recent studies indicate that eutectic high-entropy alloys can simultaneously possess high strength and high ductility, which have potential industrial applications. The present study focuses on Al0.7CoCrFeNi, a lamellar dual-phase (fcc + B2) precipitation-strengthenable eutectic high entropy alloy. This alloy exhibits an fcc + B2 (B2 with bcc nano-precipitates) microstructure resulting in a combination of the soft and ductile fcc phase together with hard B2 phase. Low temperature annealing leads to the precipitation of ordered L12 intermetallic precipitates within the fcc resulting in enhanced strength. The strengthening contribution due to fine scale L12 is modeled using Orowan dislocation bowing and by-pass mechanism. The alloy was tested under quasi-static (strain-rate = 10−3 s−1) tensile loading and dynamic (strain-rate = 103 s−1) compressive loading. Due to the fine lamellar microstructure with a large number of fcc-bcc interfaces, the alloy show relatively high flow-stresses, ~1400 MPa under quasi-static loading and in excess of 1800 MPa under dynamic loading. In this work, uniaxial tensile simulations of FCC-type Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy (as a simplified model of HEAs) are conducted in vacuum and high-temperature/pressure water environment to clarify the effect of corrosive environment on the deformation mechanisms. In vacuum, layered HCP phases are formed from FCC matrix during tensile simulation due to the generation of Shockley partial dislocations from surface and grain boundary. While, in the corrosive water environment, alloy surface is oxidized by the reactions with water and this oxidized surface layer can suppress the generation of Shockley partial dislocation as well as the resulted FCC-to-HCP phase transition; instead, generation of BCC phase is preferred to release the tensile stress and stored elastic energy, leading to an enhanced elastic modulus and reduced ductility. Thus, we revealed that the deformation mechanism of Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy is changed by the presence of high-temperature/pressure water environment—from FCC-to-HCP phase transition in vacuum to FCC-to-BCC phase transition in water. This study as a theoretical fundamental may contribute to the further improvement of HEAs with high resistance to SCC in experiments.
